overview: This two-page file concerns the decision to locate the proposed Showa Steel Works at Anshan in Japanese-controlled Manchuria rather than at Sinuiju in colonial Korea. A State Department cross-reference sheet identifies a July 1, 1930 report from Japan by Neville, while the attached extract explains that the South Manchuria Railway Company's president had discussed the project with Japan's Minister for Overseas Affairs and that subsidies and tariff advantages favored Anshan. The proposed enterprise was to be a collateral company of the railway, capitalized at ¥100 million and designed for an annual capacity of 500,000 tons.

people.name: Mitsugi Sengoku
people.role: President of the South Manchuria Railway Company

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for Neville report on the Showa Steel Works
subfiles.about: The sheet directs readers to another decimal-file location and summarizes the decision to establish the Showa Steel Works at Anshan.
subfiles.summary: This filing note cross-references document no. 189 in file 894.00 P.R./31 and identifies a July 1, 1930 report from Neville in Japan. It states that the choice between Anshan and Sinuiju was virtually settled in favor of Anshan. The proposed company would be affiliated with the South Manchuria Railway Company, with capital of ¥100 million and a capacity of 500,000 tons.

subfiles.title: Report extract on selection of Anshan for the Showa Steel Works
subfiles.about: The enclosure reports the near-final selection of Anshan over Sinuiju as the site of the proposed Showa Steel Works.
subfiles.summary: The report says that the site-selection problem was approaching resolution at the end of June. After returning to Tokyo, South Manchuria Railway president Mitsugi Sengoku discussed the matter with the Minister for Overseas Affairs, and the press subsequently reported that Anshan had effectively been chosen. Government subsidies and favorable tariff treatment helped determine the decision; the works were projected as a railway-affiliated company with ¥100 million in capital and a 500,000-ton capacity.

interest: The file gives a concise contemporary view of the institutional and financial calculations behind Japanese heavy-industrial expansion in Manchuria. Particularly useful are the explicit comparison between Anshan and Sinuiju, the role assigned to subsidies and tariff treatment, and the projected capitalization and production capacity. The cross-reference also reveals how industrial intelligence was summarized and distributed within the State Department's decimal filing system.
